analysis.one_liner: Gives taxpayers a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for donating to private school and job-training scholarships, worth up to $10 billion a year.
analysis.headline: Sen. Ted Cruz's school scholarship tax credit, backed by 16 Republican cosponsors, sat in the Senate Finance Committee for nearly two years and died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let individuals and corporations donate to private scholarship organizations and get a federal tax credit back for the full amount — up to $10 billion in donations per year would qualify, split evenly between K-12 private school scholarships and workforce training scholarships. Families could use the scholarships for private and religious schools, vocational training, and apprenticeships. The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who want help paying for private or religious K-12 schooling, career training, or apprenticeships; taxpayers with large tax bills who could redirect up to 10% of their income in taxes toward the school or training cause of their choice; and the private schools, religious schools, and scholarship-granting organizations that would receive a new multibillion-dollar funding stream.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals could claim a tax credit for cash donations to eligible scholarship organizations, up to 10% of their adjusted gross income, with unused credit carried forward for up to five years [S3].
Corporations could claim the same credit for donations, up to 5% of taxable income [S3].

Scholarship money could pay for K-12 private schooling, career and technical education, vocational training, apprenticeships, and industry certifications; the bill expressly protects the participation of private, religious, and home education providers [S3].
The scholarship allocation formula weights 80% of each year's unreserved K-12 funds by the number of children in poverty in each state, aiming money at lower-income students [S3].

Scholarships would not count as income for the student or affect eligibility for other federal programs, and the bill caps total credits at $10 billion per year, split $5 billion for school scholarships and $5 billion for workforce training [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through up to $10 billion a year in forgone revenue; and public schools, which could lose students and the per-student funding that follows them in states where scholarships shift enrollment. Because the credit is limited to a taxpayer's actual tax liability, the tax benefit flows mainly to households and corporations with substantial tax bills.

drawbacks.text: The program would cost the federal treasury up to $10 billion a year in revenue that donors redirect to causes they personally choose, with the credit limited to tax liability — so the biggest users would be taxpayers with large tax bills, not low-income households [S3].

Money would flow through private scholarship-granting organizations rather than directly to students or schools, and the bill lets organizations use a share of contributions for administration [S2][S3].

Scholarships can pay for private and religious schools, which can draw students away from public schools; the bill expressly bars federal control over private and home education providers, so public money would reach schools largely free of public accountability [S3].
States that do not submit lists of eligible organizations could have their unclaimed share reallocated to other states, pressuring states to participate in the program [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real help to students and workers — especially through the poverty-weighted funding formula and the workforce training side — but at a real cost: up to $10 billion a year in federal revenue, channeled through private organizations, with much of the tax benefit captured by affluent donors and much of the scholarship money usable at private and religious schools that the bill shields from federal oversight. Whether the trade was worth it depends heavily on how states ran the program; the bill left most of that design to the states.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, with original cosponsors including Sens. Tim Scott, Lamar Alexander, Joni Ernst, Tom Cotton, and Pat Toomey [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and it received no vote in the Senate before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].
All 16 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury kept the up to $10 billion a year it would have forgone, and public schools avoided a new private-school competitor for students and funding. Families who wanted scholarship help, and the private schools and training providers that would have received it, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and public schools kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Republican — 16 in all, plus sponsor Sen. Cruz — and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Scholarships could pay tuition at private and religious schools, creating a new multibillion-dollar customer stream paid by redirected federal tax revenue. Those schools compete with public schools for students and, under the bill, would be shielded from federal control over their practices [S3].

These nonprofits would become the permanent middlemen for up to $10 billion a year in tax-credited donations and could use a share of contributions for administration. They would control who gets scholarships and where it can be spent [S2][S3].

In states where scholarships shift enrollment to private schools, public schools would lose students and the per-student funding that follows them. The bill preserved state authority over education funding but created a competing channel for education dollars [S3].

industries.industry: Workforce training, apprenticeship, and community college providers
industries.note: Half of the credit pool was reserved for donations funding vocational training, apprenticeships, and certifications — including union-run apprenticeships — giving these providers a new funding stream for worker training [S3].
